claims.text: Elevated-temperature degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is primarily governed by the nature of its surface scale.
Oxidizing gases cause a coherent, Cr-rich oxide scale with contributions from Al and Ti to develop.
The coherent Cr-rich scale protects the underlying fcc matrix.
Protection by the Cr-rich scale maintains the alloy's overall mechanical integrity during oxidizing exposure.
Reducing gases suppress or destabilize the protective oxide scale.
Suppression or breakdown of the protective scale permits preferential oxidation of reactive Ti and Al sites.
Preferential oxidation of Ti and Al produces a more porous and less protective oxide scale.
A porous, less protective scale accelerates localized degradation.
The starting additively manufactured alloy has a homogeneous fcc matrix.
Nanoscale microstructural features in the starting alloy support high strength and fatigue performance.
Surface-scale formation mediates gas interaction with the alloy without substantially altering the bulk microstructure.
A coherent scale limits further oxygen ingress.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a stable, thin scale and a lower degradation rate than reducing exposure.
Oxidizing exposure will preserve mechanical properties relative to reducing exposure.
Reducing exposure will produce a porous, non-uniform scale and compromise local microstructural integrity relative to the starting-state baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily at approximately 700–900 °C and exposure durations on the order of hundreds of hours.
Behavior may differ at substantially different temperatures or for very short or extremely prolonged exposures.
